transcript: [00:00] AUDIO: You will hear the chair of a public meeting describing proposed traffic changes in Granford. First, you have some time to look at questions 11 to 13. Now listen carefully and answer questions 11 to 13. Good evening, everyone.

[00:50] AUDIO: I'm Phil Sutton, and I'll outline the new traffic and parking proposals before we take questions. The hospital construction brought a temporary rise in heavy vehicles, but the broader issue has lasted longer. The total volume of traffic through Granford has grown steadily. Fortunately, accident figures have not gone up, and the mix of vehicles is much the same as before.

[01:17] AUDIO: We also asked residents what troubled them most. Some expected complaints about parents driving badly near the school, and a few people mentioned noise and fumes from lorries. The strongest response, however, concerned cars left along the streets. They block sight lines and make everyday journeys inconvenient.

[01:40] AUDIO: The council can fund the signs, road markings, and other physical work. The difficult part is making sure drivers follow the new rules. We are still discussing enforcement with the police, though they support the overall plan. Before you hear the rest of the talk, you have some time to look at questions 14 to 20.

[02:35] AUDIO: Now listen and answer questions 14 to 20. Let me take you around the map. As you can see, High Street runs across the center with Station Road to the west and School Road on the eastern side. There are already traffic signals where Station Road meets High Street, so we will add another set at the opposite end, at the junction of High Street and School Road.

[03:04] AUDIO: A pedestrian crossing was considered directly outside the school. However, that would have added to congestion at drop-off time, so it will instead be placed on High Street, immediately in front of the central supermarket. At present, drivers cannot leave cars on High Street by the library. In the future, however, that restriction will be removed, allowing parking along that short section.

[03:35] AUDIO: But please keep in mind that parking at the School Road end will remain prohibited. We will also put up a new No Parking sign on School Road opposite the school entrance. This should keep the gateway clear. The disabled bays outside the High Street supermarket are sometimes occupied by delivery vehicles, so two replacement spaces will be marked in the short side road leading towards the bank.

[04:03] AUDIO: The bend on School Road just before the school is uncomfortably narrow for people walking, so to make it safer for pedestrians, the pavement there will be widened by about half a meter. Finally, the supermarket on School Road will only be allowed to receive lorries before 8 in the morning, while deliveries to the High Street supermarket will continue as usual. Okay, so that's about it. Now, would anyone...
[04:35] AUDIO: That is the end of Part 2. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

passages.title: Seed Germination
content: 📌 Stages in the experiment
transcript: [00:00] NARRATOR: You will hear two students, Emma and Jack, planning an experiment on seed germination. First, you have some time to look at questions 21 to 25. Now listen carefully and answer questions 21 to 25.
[00:51] EMMA: Have you settled on a topic for the experiment?
[00:55] JACK: I think so. I want to investigate how seeds germinate, especially whether seed size and planting method affect the result.
[01:05] EMMA: Is that connected with your future plans?

[01:08] JACK: Eventually I may work in plant science, but that is not the immediate reason. There is an optional module in the third year about seed structure and function, and I may take it. If I do, I won't be doing the dissertation module.
[01:24] EMMA: Will the experiment fit into the time we have? Germination can be slow.
[01:30] JACK: I check the schedule. If I begin this week, I can finish and analyze everything before the deadline. Several of the other possible experiments would take much longer.
[01:43] EMMA: At least it won't require unusual equipment. The laboratory has plenty of what you need.
[01:50] JACK: True. I still need to speak to the tutor before I start. I'm fairly sure the aim is suitable, and the assignment is only a small part of the final mark.
[02:01] EMMA: Five percent, I think. Not ten.
[02:04] JACK: Right. What I really need to ask is whether another student has already chosen the same topic. We are supposed to avoid duplicating a project.
[02:14] EMMA: What have you found to read?

[02:16] JACK: I started with Graves' book because people recommend it. It contains recent material, including work on modified seeds, but it was far more theoretical than I expected and difficult to use for planning a practical experiment.
[02:32] EMMA: And the journal articles?

[02:34] JACK: The one by Lee Hall examines dormant seeds after fires. I knew the basic idea already, so the conclusion was not a shock. What impressed me was the careful statistical treatment of when the fires occurred and what proportion of seeds later grew. The helpful diagrams were in a different paper.
[02:59] NARRATOR: Before you hear the rest of the discussion, you have some time to look at questions 26 to 30. Now listen and answer questions 26 to 30.
[03:44] EMMA: Let's set out the procedure. What seeds will you use?
[03:49] JACK: Vegetable seeds should be easiest to obtain. I will choose about four different types, with a range of sizes, and use several of each.
[03:59] EMMA: Before planting them, you should measure the dimensions.
[04:03] JACK: Yes, and I'll weigh every seed as well, then record both measurements.
[04:09] EMMA: What about the planting conditions?
[04:11] JACK: The soil will be the same throughout. The variable will be depth, some seeds on the surface, some a few millimeters down, and others several centimeters below it.
[04:24] EMMA: Could you put several seeds in one pot?

[04:27] JACK: That might make it hard to identify them. I'll use a separate container for each seed and give everyone a clear label. Colors could help with the labels, but they are not what I am measuring.
[04:41] EMMA: How long will you wait?
[04:43] JACK: Roughly three weeks, depending on the weather. Then I'll note which seeds have appeared and measure the height of each plant.
[04:51] EMMA: After that, you can compare the results with the original seed measurements and planting depths.
[04:58] JACK: That's right, so...
[05:03] NARRATOR: That is the end of Part 3.

passages.title: Effects Of Urban Environments On Animals
content: 📌 Effects of urban environments on animals

Introduction
Recent urban development represents a major environmental shift.
Only a few species were once considered suited to city life:
the [ _____ ], because it can adjust to many conditionsthe pigeon, because city walls resemble natural [ _____ ]
Many urban animals are actually adapting at unusual [ _____ ].

Recent research
Emilie Snell-Rood studied museum specimens of small urban mammals in Minnesota.
The size of their [ _____ ] had increased.This may reflect the need to find new sources of [ _____ ] and respond to unfamiliar dangers.
Catarina Miranda studied the [ _____ ] of urban and rural blackbirds.
City birds were often brave, but remained cautious when situations were [ _____ ].
Jonathan Atwell examined how animals react to city surroundings.
Some animals respond to [ _____ ] by producing lower hormone levels.
Sarah Partan’s team studied squirrel communication.
Urban squirrels use their [ _____ ] as a visual signal.

Long-term possibilities
Animals unique to cities may eventually develop, although some changes may not be [ _____ ].
transcript: [00:00] AUDIO: You will hear a lecturer discussing the effects of urban environments on animals. First, you have some time to look at questions 31 to 40. Now listen carefully and answer questions 31 to 40. Today I want to consider what happens to animals when towns and cities expand around them.

[00:57] AUDIO: In evolutionary terms, urban development is an enormous environmental change compressed into a very short period. It was once assumed that only a handful of species could manage city life. A familiar example is the crow, whose broad diet and flexible habits make it exceptionally adaptable. Another is the pigeon.

[01:23] AUDIO: The vertical faces of buildings provide ledges resembling the cliffs where its ancestors nested. Research now shows that these well-known species were only the first arrivals. Many animals are changing their habits and even their bodies, and the striking feature is the speed at which this is happening. At the University of Minnesota, Emily Snell Rood and her colleagues examined museum specimens of small mammals such as mice and gophers.

[01:59] AUDIO: The collections covered roughly a century, allowing urban and rural animals to be compared across time. In the city specimens, the brain had become larger while most other body measurements remained stable. That does not prove the animals are generally more intelligent. Snell Rood suggests that a more demanding environment may favor better problem solving, for example, locating unfamiliar sources of food and coping with hazards that do not occur in the countryside.

[02:36] AUDIO: In Germany, Katerina Miranda compared the behavior of urban and rural blackbirds. City birds were usually bolder around familiar threats. However, a situation that was new, something they had never encountered, still made them cautious. In a place where conditions change rapidly, that selective caution is useful.

[03:03] AUDIO: Jonathan Atwell has investigated how a range of animals respond physiologically to urban surroundings. Some populations exposed repeatedly to stress-release lower levels of certain hormones. That may be an adaptation. Reacting strongly to every passing train or siren would waste energy.

[03:26] AUDIO: A team led by Sarah Parton studied communication among squirrels. They found that city squirrels wave their tails as part of a message. Rural squirrels do this too, but the signal is more common in noisy urban places, where a visual cue can work better than sound alone. Over many generations, we might even see species that are distinctive to cities.
[03:53] AUDIO: Yet not every urban change will be permanent. If a feature is no longer useful after an animal becomes accustomed to its surroundings, natural selection may not continue to favor it.

transcript: [00:00] NARRATOR: You will hear a woman asking the secretary of a cycling club about membership and training rides. First, you have some time to look at questions 1 to 6. Now listen carefully and answer questions 1 to 6.
[00:49] JIM: Hello, South City Cycling Club. Jim speaking.
[00:54] WOMAN: Hi, I'm calling because I'd like some information about joining.
[00:58] JIM: Of course. I'm the club's secretary, Jim Hunter. Is the membership for you?
[01:06] WOMAN: Yes, it is.
[01:08] JIM: We offer two types for adults. Full membership is aimed at people who cycle seriously. It costs $260 and covers ordinary cycling as well as races in the city and around Australia.
[01:24] WOMAN: I'm not really at that level. I mainly want to join some rides when I have time.
[01:31] JIM: Then recreational membership may suit you. It's $108 for anyone over 19 and $95 for younger members.
[01:42] JIM: The fee is paid quarterly. It covers the club charge and insurance in case of an accident, though naturally we hope that is never needed.
[01:51] WOMAN: I think I'll choose recreational membership. Does that still let me take part in club activities?
[01:59] JIM: Yes, and once you join, you may wear our green and white club kit.
[02:05] WOMAN: I've noticed cyclists wearing it. Is it produced by the club?
[02:10] JIM: No, a company in Brisbane called Jerriz makes it. That's J-E-R-R-I-Z. You can order online using your membership number.
[02:20] WOMAN: Could you tell me about the training rides?

[02:23] JIM: Certainly. We run the most mornings, and they're a good way to develop both fitness and general cycling ability. We have three levels. Level A riders average at least 30 or 35 kilometers an hour.
[02:39] JIM: If you can manage about 25, Level B is probably right. Level C averages roughly 15.
[02:48] WOMAN: Level B sounds right. When do those sessions meet?
[02:53] JIM: There are two each week. Tuesday's ride begins at 5.30 a.m. with everyone meeting outside the stadium.
[03:02] WOMAN: Very early. And the other ride?
[03:06] JIM: It is also at 5.30 on Thursday, but the meeting point is the main entrance to the park.
[03:12] WOMAN: Is that just beyond the shopping center?
[03:15] JIM: Yes, exactly.
[03:20] NARRATOR: Before you hear the rest of the conversation, you have some time to look at questions 7 to 10. Now listen and answer questions 7 to 10.
[04:05] WOMAN: How long do the rides usually last?
[04:08] JIM: Around 90 minutes, so they're easy to fit in before work. Afterwards, members often stop somewhere for coffee, which makes the ride quite social.
[04:19] WOMAN: That sounds ideal. I'm new to the city and don't know many people yet.
[04:25] JIM: It is an excellent way to meet others.
[04:27] WOMAN: Does every ride have a leader?
[04:30] JIM: Not always. The riders support one another, so a leader is not essential.
[04:37] WOMAN: How do we know where to go?
[04:39] JIM: The website shows a clearly marked route for every ride. Print it beforehand and take it with you. The route changes from one week to the next.
[04:50] WOMAN: What equipment should I bring?
[04:52] JIM: Water and your phone. Do not use the phone while riding, of course, but keep it with you. In winter, we leave before sunrise, so your bicycle must also have lights.
[05:06] WOMAN: Great. I'd definitely like to join. What should I do next?
[05:12] JIM: You can...
[05:15] NARRATOR: That is the end of part one.

content: 🎧 HƯỚNG DẪN NGHE PART 2: "Company Volunteering Project"

Bấm nút Play trên trình phát Audio phía trên để nghe bài thu âm chuẩn quốc tế và hoàn thành các câu hỏi ở cột bên phải. Bạn có thể chuyển sang tab "Transcript Hội Thoại" để đối chiếu lời thoại chi tiết và bấm giờ từng câu.
transcript: [00:00] AUDIO: You will hear a staff member giving colleagues information about the company's volunteering program. First, you have some time to look at questions 11 to 16. Now listen carefully and answer questions 11 to 16. Thanks for coming.

[00:54] AUDIO: This meeting is for new employees and anyone who has not previously joined one of our volunteering projects. The company has allowed staff to spend some paid working time helping local charities for the past five years and the program has been very successful. Taking part does not require a huge commitment. The company pays for eight hours of your time each year.

[01:20] AUDIO: You can use it all on one day or divide it into two shorter sessions during the year. You may also volunteer in your own time for a few hours every week. That choice depends entirely on you. Most staff already have family commitments and other responsibilities.

[01:39] AUDIO: Feedback from employees has been extremely positive. They said the volunteering made their jobs feel more worthwhile rather than making promotion more likely. Many also enjoyed meeting people in the community and improving relationships with colleagues. One or two even found it useful to have on their CVs.

[02:00] AUDIO: A particularly successful activity last year was a get working project. The unemployed participants could already complete job applications and had strong literacy skills. What they found difficult was communicating effectively with possible employers and customers. So that was where our staff concentrated their help.

[02:24] AUDIO: This year we are starting an additional project. Until now, our main work has involved education and training, including reading support in schools and cooperation with charities. We will continue those activities, but we have agreed to look after part of a nearby park. It is a completely new direction for us.

[02:48] AUDIO: Our annual digital inclusion day takes place next month. Its purpose is to help older people remain comfortable with technology. This year it will be held at Hill College in the ICT suite. Staff volunteers will be needed to assist with the event.

[03:05] AUDIO: If you would like to participate, complete the online form. You do not need to attend the training session because each volunteer will be paired with an experienced colleague. Your manager can tell you the available dates if necessary. Before you hear the rest of the talk, you have some time to look at questions 17 to 20.

[04:02] AUDIO: Now listen and answer questions 17 to 20. The people attending last year's digital inclusion day benefited a great deal. Most were in their 70s, although some were younger and several were already in their 90s. A number owned a computer and also had a mobile phone, but both devices tended to be old models.

[04:28] AUDIO: They generally understood simple operations, such as sending a text, but at first they showed little interest in exploring anything unfamiliar. Participants said the event helped them feel less isolated, although that was not the main purpose of the day. The clearest outcome was that communicating with relatives became easier, especially through video calls. Some enjoyed shopping online, but that was not the activity they considered most useful.

[05:00] AUDIO: Playing online games was unexpectedly popular as well. A number asked about reading newspapers on tablets, which had not been covered in the session. The weather was poor, but overall the event went extremely well. That is the end of part two.

passages.title: Planning a presentation on nanotechnology
content: 🎧 HƯỚNG DẪN NGHE PART 3: "Planning a presentation on nanotechnology"

Bấm nút Play trên trình phát Audio phía trên để nghe bài thu âm chuẩn quốc tế và hoàn thành các câu hỏi ở cột bên phải. Bạn có thể chuyển sang tab "Transcript Hội Thoại" để đối chiếu lời thoại chi tiết và bấm giờ từng câu.
transcript: [00:00] NARRATOR: You will hear a tutor discussing a class presentation on nanotechnology with a student named Russ. First, you have some time to look at questions 21 to 25. Now listen carefully and answer questions 21 to 25.
[00:50] TUTOR: Come in, Russ.
[00:51] RUSS: Thanks.
[00:51] TUTOR: You wanted advice about your class presentation on nanotechnology, is that right?

[00:57] RUSS: Yes. The main difficulty is knowing what I should be aiming for. I do not have to prepare it until next week, so there is time and I can read more if necessary. But I have not been given a clear sense of what a particularly successful presentation would accomplish.
[01:17] TUTOR: You could keep your purpose simple and precise.
[01:20] RUSS: That would help.
[01:22] TUTOR: Remember that nanotechnology is something the audience has heard about, so a chronological account is unnecessary.
[01:30] RUSS: Right.
[01:32] TUTOR: Instead of covering the whole field, concentrate on one application and examine it properly.
[01:38] RUSS: For instance, the camera display coating that repels water or an additive that increases the strength of concrete.
[01:48] TUTOR: Exactly. You could equally choose a specialist field such as medicine or space research, but keep the talk focused on that single area.
[01:57] RUSS: I had been thinking about medicine.
[02:01] TUTOR: That could work. Have you planned any slides?
[02:04] RUSS: Not yet. I thought I might include quite a few images and perhaps a video.
[02:10] TUTOR: Be careful. Presenters often use visuals simply because they can. For a short talk like this, think seriously about leaving slides out altogether unless one is genuinely essential.
[02:23] RUSS: I see. My other concern was the opening.
[02:28] TUTOR: You could begin with, First I'll discuss its uses, then I'll explain how it is produced.
[02:35] RUSS: That sounds rather obvious.
[02:37] TUTOR: It would be acceptable if you had an hour, but your talk is only ten minutes. Start with something that immediately captures attention.
[02:46] RUSS: Maybe a striking picture, a surprising statistic, or a challenging question.
[02:53] TUTOR: Yes, something appropriate for this audience.
[02:57] RUSS: What should I do next? I had planned to draft the talk today and then revise it.

[03:02] TUTOR: Look again at the notes you already have. Select one important idea and express it as a single short sentence. It may take several attempts to produce exactly the right wording. Then build the rest of the talk around it.
[03:18] TUTOR: You can adjust the sentence later if needed.
[03:25] NARRATOR: Before you hear the rest of the discussion, you have some time to look at questions 26 to 30. Now listen and answer questions 26 to 30.
[04:11] TUTOR: Now let us consider the presentation you gave last term. It was on only one topic, correct?
[04:19] RUSS: Yes, an experiment I was involved in. That worked quite differently.
[04:23] TUTOR: In certain respects it was stronger than this one. The structure was easy to follow, but it ended without a proper conclusion.
[04:33] RUSS: That is reassuring.
[04:35] TUTOR: Your eye contact, however, was poor because you kept looking down at the notes. You need to face the audience and occasionally look at individual people.
[04:45] RUSS: I understand.

[04:47] TUTOR: Your body language was somewhat stiff. When showing a slide, you turned your back on the audience so that you could point to it. A better approach is to stand to one side and keep facing them.
[05:01] RUSS: I did not realize that.
[05:03] TUTOR: Your choice of words caused problems. You used several highly technical terms without explaining them, so parts of the audience struggled.
[05:13] RUSS: That took a lot of preparation.
[05:16] TUTOR: Finally, your handouts were not very helpful during the talk because the material was not in a sensible order. However, as a summary for later revision, they could still be useful.
[05:30] RUSS: I see.
[05:32] TUTOR: That is what I suggest you improve for next week.
[05:35] RUSS: Thank you. This has been very useful.
[05:38] TUTOR: I look forward to seeing the improvement then.
[05:45] NARRATOR: That is the end of Part 3.

transcript: [00:00] AUDIO: You will hear part of a lecture about episodic memory. First, you have some time to look at questions 31 to 40. Now listen carefully and answer questions 31 to 40. Today we will continue our series on memory by examining episodic memory and the way it functions.

[00:57] AUDIO: Episodic memory is our memory for an event or episode. It enables us to recall details about things that happened, including when an event occurred and its location. To understand this, think about remembering the last time you ate at a restaurant. Remembering the time, your companions, and what you ordered are all examples of episodic memory.

[01:23] AUDIO: This is different from semantic memory, sometimes called factual memory. The general knowledge we share about the world, such as what a word means. If you build on an earlier example, knowing where you left your car is episodic, but understanding how a car works comes from semantic memory. Unlike episodic memory, semantic memory is not tied to personal experience.

[01:53] AUDIO: We can view episodic memory as a process with three stages. Encoding, consolidation, and retrieval. Encoding is the first stage. It involves receiving and registering information, which is necessary for forming memories of events.

[02:14] AUDIO: The amount of attention given to an event while it happens strongly affects how successfully it is encoded. Distraction can make encoding inefficient. Encoding also depends on context. Remembering a name is often easier if you connect it with other information about the person.

[02:36] AUDIO: The next stage is consolidation, the process by which encoded memories are strengthened, stabilized, and stored for later use. Consolidation works most effectively when the information is stored as part of a network of related information. It is possible to keep memories for later retrieval without a conscious strategy. The frequency with which you retrieve them can also affect their strength.

[03:06] AUDIO: Memories may fade or become harder to access if they are not used often. The final stage is retrieval, when stored information is consciously recalled. Retrieval frequently depends on context or a prompt. For instance, when trying to remember where you parked, you may use the color of a sign near the car.

[03:31] AUDIO: This can mentally return you to the moment when you parked. A wide range of neurological and medical conditions can affect episodic memory, from Alzheimer's disease and schizophrenia to autism. Impairment can have a profound effect on everyday life. Symptoms of schizophrenia may be reduced when computer-assisted games designed to keep the brain active are used, although episodic memory may still be limited, and returning to work or study can remain difficult.

[04:09] AUDIO: Episodic memories can also help people form social connections, for example, by sharing personal details about the past. Some individuals with autism often have difficulty with this. One possible reason is the absence of a sense of self, which is essential for storing this kind of memory, and has been found to be impaired in children with autism. Research suggests that treatments aimed at improving memory may also support social development.
[04:43] AUDIO: One study examined. That is the end of Part 4.

transcript: [00:00] NARRATOR: You will hear a man asking a woman for advice about moving to Banford City. First, you have some time to look at questions 1 to 5. Now listen carefully and answer questions 1 to 5.
[00:49] LINDA: Hello, Linda speaking.
[00:51] MATT: Hi Linda, my name is Matt Brooks. Alex White passed on your number and said you might be able to advise me about relocating to Banford.
[01:00] LINDA: Yes, Alex told me you might call. What would you like to know?
[01:05] MATT: To begin with, I am trying to decide which part of the city to live in.
[01:11] LINDA: I am in Dalton. It is a pleasant suburb. The prices are not too high and there is a good park nearby.
[01:19] MATT: That sounds promising. Roughly what would a two-bedroom flat cost there each month?
[01:26] LINDA: You should find a decent place for about £850 a month. That is the usual figure. I would not pay anything above £900 and remember that bills are separate.
[01:38] MATT: That seems reasonable. I will look there. How easy is it to get around from Dalton?
[01:44] LINDA: I am fortunate because my office is in the center so I do not need public transport. I use my bike.
[01:51] MATT: I would love to do that. Is cycling in the city safe?
[01:56] LINDA: Yes, it is fine and it keeps me fit. Driving into the center is much worse because parking is extremely limited. The roads are busy at rush hour too.
[02:09] MATT: I will work at home, although I need to travel to London once or twice a week.
[02:14] LINDA: Then you will be fine. A fast train leaves for London every 30 minutes and the journey takes only about 45 minutes.
[02:24] MATT: Good.

[02:25] LINDA: The weekday service is quite reliable and trains continue until late. Weekends are the problem. Engineering work often means taking a bus to Hadham and catching the train from there, which adds a lot of time. Apart from that, I really enjoy living in Banford.
[02:47] NARRATOR: Before you hear the rest of the conversation, you have some time to look at questions 6 to 10. Now listen and answer questions 6 to 10.
[03:32] LINDA: The center has several good restaurants and a new cinema opened only a couple of months ago. There is also an arts center.
[03:40] MATT: It sounds as though Banford has nearly everything.

[03:43] LINDA: We are lucky. The schools are good and the hospital has an excellent national reputation. Everyone I know who has used it speaks highly of the care. I can also give you the details of my dentist on Bridge Street.
[03:59] LINDA: I have gone there for years without any trouble.
[04:02] MATT: That would be useful, thanks.
[04:04] LINDA: I will look up the number and send it to you.
[04:08] MATT: Great, thank you.
[04:10] LINDA: Will you be visiting Banford soon?
[04:12] MATT: Yes, my wife and I are coming next week to meet a few estate agents.
[04:17] LINDA: I can meet you and show you around if you would like.
[04:20] MATT: Are you sure? We would really appreciate it.
[04:24] LINDA: Tuesday or Thursday would suit me, as long as it is after 5.30. Thursday would be better.
[04:31] MATT: On Tuesday I have to be home before 6.
[04:34] LINDA: Thursday it is. Tell me which train you are taking and I will wait in the cafe opposite the station. It is beside the museum, so it is easy to find.
[04:46] MATT: Perfect. I will text you next week. Thanks for all your help.
[04:51] LINDA: You are welcome. See you next week.
[04:56] NARRATOR: That is the end of Part 1.

content: 🎧 HƯỚNG DẪN NGHE PART 2: "Physical Activities"

transcript: [00:00] AUDIO: You will hear a speaker giving advice about choosing physical activities. First, you have some time to look at questions 11 to 16. Now listen carefully and answer questions 11 to 16. If you still have not found an activity that suits you, there are several things worth considering before you choose.

[00:59] AUDIO: First, think about whether you would like exercising in a gym. Some people dislike having to fit a visit around a busy schedule and popular gyms can be packed unless you go very early or quite late. The advantage is that regular sessions can produce noticeable results in a fairly short period. Running has grown enormously in popularity.

[01:25] AUDIO: One reason is that almost anybody can begin, even if at first they can manage only a few metres. Do buy suitable shoes though. A well-made pair is worth the money, even if it is not cheap. You can run at almost any hour, although snow or ice may prevent you.

[01:46] AUDIO: Swimming is also excellent for improving fitness. Many people choose it because an indoor pool is available throughout the year. The downside is that it can feel repetitive and lonely, since it is difficult to talk while swimming lengths. Cycling is now nearly as popular as running.

[02:08] AUDIO: Besides improving fitness, it gives people the pleasure of being outdoors in a park or the countryside. Naturally, the weather needs to be reasonable. Only the most committed cyclists go out in heavy rain and wind. Yoga may appeal if you want to develop both mental and physical health.

[02:30] AUDIO: It builds strength and, with a competent teacher, it carries a lower risk of injury than many more vigorous sports. That does not mean it is effortless. People with limited flexibility often find it demanding. Another possibility is to work with a personal trainer.

[02:52] AUDIO: It can be expensive, but having someone to encourage you and guide you towards your targets makes it easier to keep going. Check that the trainer has a recognised qualification, because poor instruction can cause lasting harm. Before you hear the rest of the talk, you have some time to look at questions 17 to 20. Now listen and answer questions 17 to 20.

[03:58] AUDIO: Whatever activity you choose, do not buy a gym membership unless you are confident you will use it. Many people pay for months and then attend only a few times. Why do their intentions disappear? I do not believe they suddenly become too busy or stop caring about fitness.

[04:20] AUDIO: More often, slow progress damages their confidence and they begin to think their target is beyond them. They also underestimate how much determination and sustained effort weekly training requires. Many simply cannot maintain that level of commitment. Setting manageable goals can help.

[04:44] AUDIO: Be realistic rather than pushing yourself too far. Some people recommend putting every goal in writing, but I prefer a flexible plan. Each time you reach a target, reward yourself with something you really enjoy. And if you have a setback, do not treat it as failure.
[05:05] AUDIO: Any long-term programme will include difficult periods. That is the end of part two.

transcript: [00:00] NARRATOR: You will hear a student discussing a textile design project with his tutor. First, you have some time to look at questions 21 to 24. Now listen carefully and answer questions 21 to 24.
[00:50] TUTOR: All right, Jim. You wanted to talk about your textile design project?
[00:55] JIM: Yes. I have been investigating how natural dyes can color materials such as cotton and wool.
[01:03] TUTOR: What made you choose that subject?

[01:06] JIM: The textile exhibition at the museum gave me several useful ideas, and color has always interested me. But the first thing that really caught my attention was years ago when I visited a carpet shop in Turkey with my parents. The rugs had extraordinary colors.
[01:25] TUTOR: Some of those colors may have come from synthetic dyes.
[01:29] JIM: Possibly. Once I had chosen the project, I found an excellent book about a Californian botanic garden that grows plants used in dyeing.
[01:40] TUTOR: Your project also needed a practical investigation.
[01:45] JIM: It did. At first, I could not decide which variables to use. My original plan was to take one fiber, perhaps cotton, And test it with several dyes? Exactly.
[02:01] JIM: Then I broadened the study and included wool and nylon as well as cotton.
[02:06] TUTOR: Were you still using only one dye?
[02:09] JIM: No, I used a variety, including a few synthetic dyes, so I could compare the results.
[02:16] TUTOR: I see.
[02:18] JIM: I carried out the experiments last week. Some natural dyes were ready-made and arrived quickly from an online supplier, while I prepared others myself.
[02:28] TUTOR: That sounds time-consuming.
[02:31] JIM: It was. I assumed I would need only a small spoonful of raw material. But I was completely wrong. For a red dye made from beetroot, I had to cut up a large heap of it.
[02:44] JIM: Preparing everything took far longer than expected.
[02:48] TUTOR: Food coloring is another option.
[02:51] JIM: I tried one artificial yellow coloring.
[02:55] TUTOR: Tartrazine?
[02:56] JIM: Yes. On cotton, it initially produced a strong color, but the color disappeared as soon as I rinsed the cloth. I had planned to test it on nylon, too, but I decided not to continue.
[03:10] TUTOR: Were you concerned about health risks?
[03:13] JIM: I assumed an approved food coloring would be harmless.
[03:17] TUTOR: It is usually safe, although a small number of people can have an allergic reaction.
[03:26] NARRATOR: Before you hear the rest of the discussion, you have some time to look at questions 25 to 30. Now listen and answer questions 25 to 30.
[04:12] TUTOR: Which natural dyes did you investigate?
[04:15] JIM: One was turmeric. It creates a vivid yellow and is commonly used in foods such as curry.
[04:23] TUTOR: It may have health benefits when eaten, but as a fabric dye, it often fades after only a few washes.
[04:31] JIM: I also put beetroot dye on wool. Beetroot stains my hands bright red whenever I prepare it, so I expected a similar result. Instead, the wool turned a thin, creamy color.
[04:45] TUTOR: Did you read about Tyrian purple?
[04:48] JIM: Yes. It is obtained from shellfish, and because it was exceptionally rare, only powerful people wore it in ancient times. I could not use it.
[05:00] TUTOR: It disappeared from use centuries ago, though a modern researcher recently obtained a little. Chemical dyes can now create the same purple. What about black dyes?
[05:13] JIM: I tried logwood. The process was complicated because I had to treat the cloth first, so it would absorb the color.
[05:23] TUTOR: I hope you wore gloves.
[05:25] JIM: Yes. I knew it could be dangerous.
[05:27] TUTOR: Good. Swallowing logwood dye can be extremely poisonous. Did you consider an insect-based color such as cochineal?
[05:36] JIM: Yes. I did not make it myself. Crushing insects would have taken too long, and they are not found locally. The prepared dye was easy to order online, but it was extremely expensive.
[05:51] TUTOR: It is powerful, which is why cooks use only tiny amounts, and it is rarely chosen for textiles.
[05:59] JIM: I also read that iron oxide can color fabric if the metal is allowed to rust while touching it.

[06:07] TUTOR: That method works on cotton, but the metal can weaken the cloth, so material treated this way may not last long. The shades are also rather subtle, which some people dislike. You have clearly done a great deal of work.
[06:27] NARRATOR: That is the end of part three.

transcript: [00:00] AUDIO: You will hear a lecturer describing research on the sleepy lizard. First, you have some time to look at questions 31 to 40. Now listen carefully and answer questions 31 to 40. Last week we began our study of reptiles with crocodiles and snakes.

[00:56] AUDIO: Today we will turn to a different reptile, the lizard, focusing on research into a species whose Latin name is Tiliqua rugosa. It is usually called the sleepy lizard because it moves slowly and spends long periods resting beneath rocks or warming itself in the sun. Let me begin with its appearance. Sleepy lizards are widespread in Western and South Australia.

[01:25] AUDIO: Whereas most European lizards are small, green, and quick, this species is brown. Its most recognizable feature is its dark blue tongue, which contrasts sharply with the bright pink interior of its mouth. It is also considerably larger than most European species. Its diet is varied and includes insects and even small animals, although plants make up the largest part.

[01:55] AUDIO: Despite their size and powerful jaws, which can break beetles and snail shells, sleepy lizards have several predators. In the past, large birds such as cassowaries were a major threat. Today, snakes are more likely to catch and kill them. Cars are another serious danger because many lizards die while crossing roads.

[02:21] AUDIO: Michael Freak of Flinders University conducted a study of how these animals navigate. Although they travel slowly, they can cover substantial distances. He moved some lizards away from their territory and found that they generally returned home if they had a clear view of the sky. They did not appear to rely on landmarks at ground level.

[02:47] AUDIO: Field observations have also revealed unusual mating behavior. Unlike most animals, sleepy lizards appear to be largely monogamous, reuniting with the same partner for several years. A male and female remain together for an extended period both before and after their young hatch. Why might they do this?

[03:12] AUDIO: One possibility is that two adults improve the young lizard's chances of survival. However, researchers have seen almost no contact between parents and offspring once the eggs have hatched, so the evidence does not support that explanation. A second idea comes from the fact that males in these long-term pairs are often larger and stronger than other males. The male may remain with the female to provide protection from competing males, though this has not been proved.

[03:46] AUDIO: Finally, I want to describe a tracking project in which I took part. We captured wild lizards and fitted each one with a very small GPS unit attached to its tail. After releasing them, we followed their movements for 12 days. The equipment recorded not only location but also the number of steps each animal took.

[04:11] AUDIO: The results contained one unexpected pattern. The lizards met far less often than we had predicted. They seemed to be keeping away from one another. We cannot yet be certain why, but one hypothesis is that fights between males can cause serious injuries.
[04:32] AUDIO: Avoidance may therefore reduce the risk of injury and serve as a form of self-preservation. Much more evidence is needed before we can confirm this. That is the end of Part 4.

transcript: [00:00] NARRATOR: You will hear a woman asking a former trainee about his experience at a company. First, you have some time to look at questions 1 to 7. Now listen carefully and answer questions 1 to 7.
[00:50] MARTHA: Hello, Alex. It's Martha Clines. James White gave me your number. I hope it's alright to call.
[00:58] ALEX: Of course. How are you, Martha?
[01:02] MARTHA: Fine, thanks. I'm calling because I could use some advice.
[01:06] ALEX: Sure. What about?
[01:09] MARTHA: The training scheme you completed at JPNW a few years ago. I'm applying for the same programme.
[01:17] ALEX: Oh, yes. I finished mine in 2014. It was one of the best decisions I've made and I still work there.
[01:27] MARTHA: Really? Which area are you in now?
[01:31] ALEX: I'm in customer services now, but my original placement was in finance. I spent my first two years there before transferring to my present department.
[01:44] MARTHA: Customer services is where I'm hoping to train. Did you like the programme?

[01:49] ALEX: I was quite anxious at first. My school exam results weren't strong and I was especially worried because I hadn't passed maths. In practice, that wasn't a problem because I took plenty of courses at work.
[02:08] MARTHA: Did you receive a diploma when the training ended? I'm thinking of choosing the one in business skills.
[02:15] ALEX: Yes, and that sounds like a sensible choice. I did the IT skills diploma, but looking back, I wish I'd taken business instead.
[02:27] MARTHA: That's useful to know. How did you get along with the other trainees?
[02:32] ALEX: About 20 of us began together and our ages were quite close. I was 18. Only one trainee was younger, at 17. Everyone else was between 18 and 20 and I made some good friends.
[02:52] MARTHA: People say there are plenty of opportunities at JPNW.
[02:56] ALEX: There are. Because it's such a large organisation, you can gain experience in many different areas.
[03:05] MARTHA: And what about the pay? I understand trainees earn a lower minimum wage than regular staff.

[03:12] ALEX: That's true, and it isn't ideal. However, trainees receive exactly the same amount of holiday as permanent employees. If the company offers you a job afterwards, the salary rises considerably.
[03:30] MARTHA: The money isn't my main reason for applying. I want the experience and I've heard the year gives people much more confidence.
[03:39] ALEX: It certainly does. That was the biggest benefit for me. The work is varied as well, so you're given many different tasks. I even enjoyed the studying.
[03:53] MARTHA: Do trainees spend any time at college?
[03:56] ALEX: Yes, one day every month. You get support from both your college tutor and your manager at work.
[04:05] MARTHA: Good. The company is easy to reach too, isn't it?
[04:10] ALEX: Yes. It's very near the railway station, so its location is a real advantage.
[04:21] NARRATOR: Before you hear the rest of the conversation, you have some time to look at questions 8 to 10. Now listen and answer questions 8 to 10.
[05:07] ALEX: Have they given you an interview date yet?
[05:10] MARTHA: Yes, the 23rd of this month.
[05:13] ALEX: If you prepare properly, you shouldn't be too worried. The interviewers are very friendly.
[05:21] MARTHA: I'm uncertain about what to wear. What would you suggest?
[05:25] ALEX: Don't choose anything too casual, such as jeans. A smart jacket with a skirt or trousers would be fine.
[05:35] MARTHA: Right, thanks. Do you have any other advice?

[05:40] ALEX: One obvious thing is to arrive with time to spare. They really dislike candidates who are late, so check exactly how long the journey takes. And another tip my manager gave me before my interview was to smile. Even if you're nervous, it helps people react positively to you.
[06:04] MARTHA: I'll need to practice that in front of the mirror.
[06:07] ALEX: Good luck then. Let me know if you need anything else.
[06:12] MARTHA: Thanks very much.

Bấm nút Play trên trình phát Audio phía trên để nghe bài thu âm chuẩn quốc tế và hoàn thành các câu hỏi ở cột bên phải. Bạn có thể chuyển sang tab "Transcript Hội Thoại" để đối chiếu lời thoại chi tiết và bấm giờ từng câu.
transcript: [00:00] AUDIO: You will hear a guide welcoming visitors to a snow and ski center. First, you have some time to look at questions 11 to 16. Now listen carefully and answer questions 11 to 16. Hello everyone and welcome to the snow center.

[00:55] AUDIO: I'm Annie. I hope the coach journey from the airport was pleasant. As you can see, we've had plenty of fresh snow. You've arrived at New Zealand's leading snow and ski center and we've arranged a full week of activities.

[01:12] AUDIO: Cross-country skiing is what most guests come for. It generally takes place on fairly level ground rather than steep mountain slopes. We have marked routes, but I'd really recommend leaving the normal trails and exploring independently at least once. You can choose your own pace, push hard for an excellent aerobic workout, or move gently and take in the views.

[01:41] AUDIO: This afternoon, you're going dog sledding. You may have watched our dogs racing in the Winter Sled Festival on television recently. On today's trip, anyone who wants to may take charge of a team and learn to drive the dogs while following our trail leader. If that doesn't appeal, you can simply travel as a passenger and enjoy the ride.

[02:06] AUDIO: At the weekend, we hold a team relay, and every one of you is invited. A nearby school will also attend, with several teachers competing. The emphasis is on joining in, not on winning, so each participant receives a medal. Teams contain between two and four people, and every team completes four circuits of the course.

[02:33] AUDIO: Your final outing is a snowshoe expedition on Mount Frenner. The special shoes let you walk over the surface of the snow. Miners once searched the area for gold, although little evidence of the old workings remains. In summer, when the snow disappears, the slopes are covered in unusual plants and flowers.

[02:56] AUDIO: Your route is a long but fairly gentle climb, and walkers normally need two days to reach the summit and return. You'll stay overnight in our mountain hut, and that accommodation is part of your package. The hut has comfortable beds, a fireplace, and a supply of drinking water. Please use melted snow for washing so the water is conserved.

[03:22] AUDIO: We can carry your luggage up by snowmobile for $10 per person. Cooking equipment is provided, but you'll need to bring your own food for the evening and morning meals. Storms can be severe on Mount Frenner. If one arrives, remain in the hut until conditions improve.

[03:41] AUDIO: They usually pass quickly. Don't worry about missing the airport coach, because it probably won't be operating either. There is an emergency locator beacon in the hut, but activate it only for a genuine emergency, such as illness or injury. Before you hear the rest of the talk, you have some time to look at questions 17 to 20.

[04:41] AUDIO: Now listen and answer questions 17 to 20. Now I'll explain the different ski trails you can use while you're here. Highland Trail begins right beside the center. It was planned so that first-time skiers can enjoy it, whatever their age or level, but experienced visitors also use it to practice technique.

[05:08] AUDIO: Next is Pine Trail. If you're unsure of your skiing, this one is best left to experts. The route follows a steep valley with a river far below. It can feel frightening, but it's very enjoyable once you've mastered the skills required for hills.

[05:27] AUDIO: Stony Trail is suitable after you've learned the basics. It has one or two difficult stretches, but nothing too demanding. Halfway along, there's a shelter where you can sit down, rest, and enjoy the afternoon sunshine. Finally, Loser's Trail starts in a gentle river valley, but its last section is exposed, and snow conditions can be difficult.
[05:54] AUDIO: In snow or strong wind, ask us whether the route is open before setting off. All right, please come with me and we'll begin.

content: 🎧 HƯỚNG DẪN NGHE PART 3: "Nutritional Information On Food Packaging"

Bấm nút Play trên trình phát Audio phía trên để nghe bài thu âm chuẩn quốc tế và hoàn thành các câu hỏi ở cột bên phải. Bạn có thể chuyển sang tab "Transcript Hội Thoại" để đối chiếu lời thoại chi tiết và bấm giờ từng câu.
transcript: [00:00] NARRATOR: You will hear two students discussing a project on nutritional information printed on food packaging. First, you have some time to look at questions 21 to 26. Now listen carefully and answer questions 21 to 26.
[00:53] JACK: I've still got a great deal to finish for our report on nutrition labels.
[00:58] ALICE: So, have I? What has the project shown you about the way you shop?

[01:05] JACK: Because I'm allergic to peanuts, I've always examined that part of a label very carefully. Apart from checking for traces of nuts, though, I hardly ever read enough of the information to judge whether a product was healthy.

[01:19] ALICE: The project has made me much more careful, too. I used to accept claims such as low in fat without question. Now I've discovered that the supposedly healthy yogurt I've bought for years contains a lot of sugar and is fairly high in calories.
[01:37] JACK: Ready meals were the worst. Comparing several supermarket pizzas was particularly revealing. I couldn't believe how many calories they had.
[01:47] ALICE: Yes, and if you don't study the label closely, you miss the fact that the nutritional figures apply to only half a pizza.
[01:56] JACK: Even though most people eat the whole one. That presentation of the information is hardly transparent.
[02:04] ALICE: True. Will it make you stop buying pizza?
[02:08] JACK: Probably not. I did enjoy comparing the labeling systems used by different manufacturers. The particular system can make a considerable difference.
[02:19] ALICE: Which format did you like best?

[02:22] JACK: The traditional daily value system. It shows what share of your recommended daily intake is supplied by each ingredient. It may not be the quickest system to understand, but it gives the complete picture. I want to see every ingredient, not only the amounts of fat, salt, and sugar.
[02:45] ALICE: At least supermarkets are trying to give customers dependable information.
[02:50] JACK: Yes, although the systems used by different chains need to be more consistent, especially over serving sizes.
[02:57] ALICE: The labels on the various brands of chicken flavor crisps were revealing as well.
[03:03] JACK: They certainly were. I can't see how a product can be called chicken flavor when it contains only artificial additives.
[03:13] ALICE: Exactly. I would have expected at least a small amount of actual chicken.
[03:19] JACK: Definitely.
[03:21] ALICE: Overall, don't you think nutritional labeling is a useful idea? I imagine it could change behavior and prevent parents, in particular, from buying unsuitable products.
[03:33] JACK: But didn't the study suggest the reverse? People didn't necessarily give up on healthy products.
[03:41] ALICE: It only suggested that this might happen. The findings are not decisive, and the study involved very few people. More research is clearly needed.
[03:53] JACK: Yes, you're probably right.
[03:58] NARRATOR: Before you hear the rest of the discussion, you have some time to look at questions 27 to 30. Now listen and answer questions 27 to 30.
[04:46] JACK: What did you think about the traffic light labels?
[04:50] ALICE: Supermarkets seem to like the color-coded approach, using red, orange, and green to show the levels of fat, sugar, and salt.
[04:59] JACK: Yet it hasn't been introduced everywhere or placed on every product. Why do you think that is?
[05:07] ALICE: Food manufacturers have applied pressure. It's understandable that some companies object to labels that draw attention to how unhealthy their products are.
[05:18] JACK: I'd assumed the system was compulsory, so I was amazed to discover that supermarkets can choose whether to use it.
[05:26] ALICE: So was I. What surprised me even more was that it was launched without enough research or consultation. Many specialists had serious reservations.
[05:38] JACK: That is strange. Perhaps research is easier now that shoppers know the system.
[05:45] ALICE: Possibly.
[05:46] JACK: The survey participants were generally positive about traffic light labels.
[05:52] ALICE: Yes, but I don't think the researchers chose the most relevant people. They should have concentrated on those with low literacy, because the labels are meant to be accessible to them.
[06:04] JACK: Still, it was useful to receive opinions from every socioeconomic group, and the responses didn't differ much between those groups.
[06:13] ALICE: True. However, interviewing everyone face-to-face meant they could only use a much smaller sample. I wonder why they selected that method.
[06:24] JACK: I'm not sure. Were the participants chosen randomly, or did they volunteer?

passages.title: The History Of Coffee
content: 📌 The History of Coffee

Coffee in the Arab world
Wild coffee from Ethiopia was traded on a limited scale.
1522: The Ottoman court accepted coffee as a medicine.
1623: Constantinople’s ruler ordered the [ _____ ] of all the city’s coffee houses.

Coffee reaches Europe in the 17th century
Coffee shops were said to serve a similar purpose to [ _____ ].
They contributed significantly to social and [ _____ ] change.

Coffee and European colonisation
European countries developed coffee plantations in their colonies.
Varieties of coffee were frequently named after the [ _____ ] they were shipped from.
In Brazil and the Caribbean, most coffee production relied on [ _____ ].
In Java, coffee functioned as a type of [ _____ ].
Coffee became nearly as significant as [ _____ ].
Britain’s shift toward drinking [ _____ ] did not occur in the USA.

Coffee during the 19th century
Better [ _____ ] helped to reduce prices.
Industrial employees found that coffee enabled them to work at [ _____ ].
transcript: [00:00] AUDIO: You will hear a lecturer giving a presentation about the history of coffee. First, you have some time to look at questions 31 to 40. Now listen carefully and answer questions 31 to 40. In this talk, I'll consider coffee and the role it has played in both economic and social life.

[00:59] AUDIO: It is generally believed that people first drank it in the Arab world. Written records before the 16th century are extremely scarce, although that does not prove that coffee was unknown earlier. There is evidence that people initially collected coffee from wild bushes in Ethiopia in northeastern Africa. Early in the 16th century, traders began buying it, and the drink slowly spread across the Middle East.

[01:31] AUDIO: We also know that in 1522, in Constantinople, the heart of the Ottoman Empire, the court doctor authorized coffee as a medicine. By the middle of the century, coffee plants were being cultivated in Yemen. For roughly the next hundred years, that region supplied most of the coffee consumed in Africa and the Arab world. One striking feature of coffee is the way it influenced social life.

[02:02] AUDIO: People seldom drank it at home. Instead, they visited coffee houses where men in particular met to drink and exchange views about current affairs. Authorities considered these discussions potentially threatening. In 1623, Constantinople's ruler therefore ordered the destruction of every coffee house in the city.

[02:27] AUDIO: New establishments opened after he died, however, and coffee drinking continued. During the 17th century, the habit reached Europe. Coffee shops there also became meeting places where ordinary people, usually men, gathered to exchange ideas. Some observers consequently compared their function with that of universities.

[02:52] AUDIO: By bringing people together outside their homes to discuss the major issues of the day, the shops had a powerful influence on society. Numerous social movements and political changes began in coffee house conversations. Toward the end of the 17th century, Yemen lost its control over production. Coffee cultivation then expanded worldwide, assisted by European colonization.

[03:23] AUDIO: European powers created plantations in Indonesia and the Caribbean, and output from their colonies rose rapidly. Coffees produced in different locations often took names such as mocha or java from the port through which they were exported to Europe. Labor arrangements, though, varied considerably between colonies. In Brazil and a number of Caribbean colonies, coffee grew on enormous plantations worked mainly by slaves.

[03:56] AUDIO: Java followed another pattern. After the Dutch colonized the island, local farmers cultivated coffee and handed a proportion of the crop to the colonial authorities, so the beans served as a form of taxation. Regardless of the system, 18th century European rule tied coffee production closely to colonization. Growers produced ever larger quantities to satisfy European demand, and coffee became almost as important as sugar, which was cultivated under very similar conditions.

[04:35] AUDIO: Even so, prices remained too high for most people to drink coffee regularly at home. Consumption still centered on public coffee houses, and the drink retained an element of luxury. In Britain, meanwhile, tea arrived from China and gradually displaced coffee. It was initially affordable only to the wealthy, but by the late 18th century it was consumed widely.

[05:03] AUDIO: The United States, having gained independence from Britain in 1776, did not make the same change to tea. Coffee remained its preferred drink, as it is today. By the start of the 19th century, coffee was already produced and consumed on a large scale. During that century, however, output surged and prices fell.

[05:29] AUDIO: One reason was the development of cheaper, more efficient transportation. Coffee then became affordable to workers rather than remaining a middle-class drink. This coincided with industrialization across much of Europe. Factory work sometimes continued after dark, requiring employees to work through the night.
[05:51] AUDIO: Coffee's stimulating effect therefore became valuable. It was no longer simply a breakfast drink. There were also developments in cultivation.
